story.headline: Gunman kills six in Krakow's main square
story.summary: A gunman killed six people in Krakow's main market square on 7 November and three relatives at home; prosecutors are investigating a suspected terrorist offence.
story.display_body: A gunman killed six people in the main market square of Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, on Saturday 7 November, and police later found three more bodies, his father, mother and sister, at his family home. Police said the man, a Polish citizen in his mid-20s, drove into the square at about 15:00 and fired at random people from his car, moving between several spots with an automatic rifle, before he was shot by officers; he is in hospital in a critical condition. Four women and two men died in the square, among them a British national, and 16 people were wounded, including citizens of Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and the UK and two police officers. The family home is in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 km north-east of Krakow. Poland's national prosecutor's office has opened an investigation into a suspected "terrorist offence", and Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it terrorism. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultranationalistic" views; officials have not yet stated a motive. Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday 8 November. Switzerland's foreign ministry told the Keystone-SDA news agency it knows of no Swiss victims.
story.why: Tusk said Poland had never seen terrorism this drastic, and the attack hit one of Europe's busiest tourist squares.

story.headline: Herzog hands Eisenkot first shot at government
story.summary: Israel's president said he will task Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government after 67 MKs recommended him.
story.display_body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on the evening of Saturday 7 November that he will give Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, the first chance to form a government; the formal ceremony is set for 17:00 on Sunday 8 November. Herzog's office says factions with 67 of the Knesset's 120 members recommended Eisenkot, factions with 46 recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and one seven-member faction recommended no one. Under Israel's Basic Law, Eisenkot will have 28 days, plus up to 14 more if Herzog grants them, to win a majority of 61. Those 67 recommendations do not add up to a coalition: his own bloc has 48 seats, and the 67 include the two Arab parties (19 seats), which Netanyahu campaigned against relying on. SRF notes that Avigdor Lieberman, one of Eisenkot's key partners, rejects both a government that depends on Arab votes and a minority government. The other option, the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (seven seats, the faction that recommended no one), would want its young men to stay exempt from military service, which Eisenkot's camp campaigned against. The new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday 10 November, and Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a government is formed.
story.why: this is the first time since the 27 October election that someone other than Netanyahu has the mandate, but every path to 61 seats costs Eisenkot a campaign promise.

story.headline: CENTCOM extends Iran blockade to land routes
story.summary: CENTCOM set up Task Force Iron Gate against Iran's land supply routes and disabled the cargo ship M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman.
story.display_body: The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Saturday 7 November that it has set up a task force to stop Iran moving weapons and other goods over land, and that the same day its forces disabled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman for trying to break the naval blockade of Iranian ports. According to Al Jazeera, the new unit, "Task Force Iron Gate", is based in Tampa, Florida, and will work with other US agencies against the movement of "advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams" across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. The ship, the St Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, was hit at the stern by precision munitions fired from a US aircraft after the crew was told to leave the targeted areas. CENTCOM says that since July 147 ships have turned back on its orders and five that refused have been disabled. Iran's IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) navy said two oil tankers hit mines near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, and the state news agency IRNA reported explosions on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas.
story.why: Washington is extending its pressure from Iran's sea lanes to its land borders while Qatar-mediated talks continue.

story.headline: Houthi missile debris damages Aramco office in Riyadh
story.summary: Debris from intercepted Houthi missiles damaged a Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh's financial district; Houthis say coalition strikes near Sanaa killed 33.
story.display_body: An administrative building of the Saudi oil company Aramco in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District was damaged by falling debris on Sunday 8 November after Saudi air defences intercepted ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said; nobody was hurt. The Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said two missiles were aimed at Riyadh and another at the Eastern Province, and that two more missiles and a drone were destroyed over the south. El País reports that the financial district has been closed for almost a month, with staff working from home. The day before, the Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi-led coalition air strikes on the village of al-Shariyah, east of Sanaa, killed 33 people, including 13 children; the coalition has not commented and Al Jazeera could not verify the figure. The Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia since Yemen's truce collapsed in July, and Yemeni government forces launched an offensive towards Sanaa last month.

story.headline: Zaporizhzhia plant loses outside power again
story.summary: The occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant lost its last external power line on 8 November, its 16th blackout this year, as Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 in Dnipropetrovsk.
story.display_body: The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant lost its last outside power line at 02:36 on Sunday 8 November and is running on diesel generators, according to Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom, as reported by Ukrinform. Energoatom says this is the 16th complete loss of outside power at Europe's largest nuclear plant this year; the plant needs electricity to keep its nuclear fuel cool, so a failure of the backup generators could cause a radiation accident. Overnight Russian strikes on energy sites also cut power in six regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry. In Dnipropetrovsk region more than 600,000 people lost electricity and hospitals are running on generators, the regional military administration head, Oleksandr Hanja, said, as reported by Le Monde. The strikes follow the large attack on Kyiv overnight into Saturday 7 November, ahead of US–Russia–Ukraine talks due in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday 10 and Wednesday 11 November.

story.headline: Aeschi enters race to succeed Parmelin
story.summary: SVP group leader Thomas Aeschi confirmed he is running for the Federal Council seat Guy Parmelin is vacating; the election is on 9 December.
story.display_body: Thomas Aeschi, leader of the Swiss People's Party (SVP) group in the federal parliament, confirmed on Sunday 8 November that he will run to succeed Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin, two weeks after the party's internal deadline. Aeschi, 47, a national councillor from Zug, told SonntagsBlick he would like to take over asylum policy from Justice Minister Beat Jans (SP), saying the problems in asylum and migration remain "very large". The Zug SVP had already nominated him in October, and SRF counts eight SVP members who have now declared. The SVP parliamentary group picks its official ticket on Friday 20 November, and the Federal Assembly elects Parmelin's successor on Wednesday 9 December. SRF's federal correspondent calls Aeschi the party leadership's likely favourite but expects resistance from other parties, which see him as a hard-liner; Aeschi lost to Parmelin in 2015. His candidacy also makes it harder for the French-speaking candidates, Céline Amaudruz and Pierre Alain Schnegg, to reach the ticket, although French-speaking SVP members want the seat of Parmelin, a Vaudois, to stay with the Romandie.
story.why: who replaces Parmelin will decide whether the French-speaking SVP keeps its seat and could change who runs the justice and asylum department.

story.headline: Valais defends Crans-Montana aid refusals
story.summary: Valais defended refusing a CHF 60,000 emergency payment to seven Crans-Montana fire survivors who were not hospitalised overnight.
story.display_body: The canton of Valais defended its rules on Saturday 7 November after it emerged that seven survivors of the Crans-Montana fire were refused the CHF 60,000 emergency payment funded by the canton and the Confederation. Tribune de Genève and 24 heures first reported the refusals. To qualify, a person must have lost a relative or spent at least one night in hospital. Geneva lawyer Robert Assaël, who represents one of the survivors, called the hospital-night rule "completely arbitrary" on RTS: he said his client could have stayed in hospital but gave up her bed to more badly injured people. Cantonal health and social affairs minister Mathias Reynard said all victims recognised under the federal victim support law (LAVI) are entitled to help, including money, but that aid has to be graded so that families who lost children or people with lifelong injuries get more.
